problem: State-of-the-art embodied agents (about 50% on RoboTHOR ObjectNav, below 10% on RoomR rearrangement) are too unreliable to deploy. Prior help-seeking methods either use hand-designed heuristics such as model confusion, or need the underlying agent retrained with an extra ask action and reward shaping.
motivation: Agents that can ask a human for help when stuck could become reliable enough for real use, but asking is costly, so the amount of help must be minimized. The agent's recurrent belief state carries enough information to tell when it is failing, so a lightweight learned policy on top of a frozen agent can decide when to query, without touching the agent's weights.
key_idea: Train a small RL policy (MLP + GRU) on the frozen agent's GRU hidden state to choose at each step between the agent's action and an expert's action, penalizing failure and expert use, with the failure penalty embedded as an input so help frequency can be tuned at inference.
insight: A learned policy on the frozen agent's beliefs asks for help far more efficiently than random or confidence-based asking. On ObjectNav, over 90% SR needs about 17% EP with Ask4Help versus 41% with Naive Helper, and on RoomR the Naive Helper needs 70% EP and Model Confusion 63% to match 39%. The pretrained agent matters: Ask4Help with a random agent uses 98.99% EP versus 12.31% with the pretrained agent. The policy is data-efficient (10% of the scenes costs about 2% SR) and robust to noisy experts (CE-0.8 still beats no help).
method: Ask4Help policy: MLP + GRU that takes the frozen E-AI agent's GRU hidden state (beliefs) and outputs a binary choice, Agent or Expert, at each step; the expert then supplies the optimal next action.
RL training: DD-PPO for 15M steps, with gradients updating only the Ask4Help module and the underlying agent frozen. It is trained on a held-out 25% of training scenes not used to train the agent.

Reward: r = r_fail + 1_ask*r_init_ask + r_step_ask for ObjectNav (-10, -1, -0.01). The one-time initial-ask penalty is larger than the per-step penalty, since repeated queries cost less once the expert is engaged. For RoomR the sparse failure term is replaced by the RoomR rearrangement reward, with r_init_ask=-0.5 and r_step_ask=-0.02.

Preference conditioning: sample r_fail from -1 to -30 per episode (R_-1..R_-30) and feed a learned 12-d embedding of the config index to the GRU. Help frequency can then be changed at test time by changing the embedding, without retraining.

Experts: NavMesh shortest-path expert for ObjectNav, Heuristic Expert from RoomR for rearrangement. Evaluated with corrupted experts CE-eps (random action with probability eps) and 11 human participants.
Baselines: Naive Helper (Bernoulli(p) expert steps), Model Confusion (ask if the top-2 action probability gap is below eps), and a fixed M-agent-steps then N-expert-steps heuristic.

setting.backbone: EmbCLIP agent (frozen, CLIP-based ResNet-50 with GRU) plus a trained MLP+GRU Ask4Help policy
setting.training_data: EmbCLIP agent trained on 75% of training scenes (45 RoboTHOR ObjectNav scenes, 60 iTHOR RoomR scenes). Ask4Help trained with DD-PPO for 15M steps on the remaining 25% of scenes.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (agent beliefs from frozen EmbCLIP); RoomR gets current and goal-state egocentric images
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level actions (MoveAhead, RotateLeft/Right, LookUp/Down, End; RoomR adds PickUpX etc.). The Ask4Help policy makes a binary Agent/Expert choice.
setting.privileged: An expert is queried at test time: NavMesh shortest-path actions for ObjectNav, the Heuristic Expert for RoomR, or human/noisy experts.

results: Ask4Help lifts ObjectNav SR from 52.4% to 86.3% with about 12-13% expert steps, and RoomR SR from 6.9% to 90.4% (FS 95.32) with 39% EP. It dominates Naive Helper and Model Confusion at every EP level; for example, over 90% SR needs 41% EP with Naive Helper versus about 17% with Ask4Help. With a 20-step expert cap it reaches 70% SR versus 61% for Model Confusion.
limitations: The agent is frozen, so it cannot learn from expert feedback and may query the expert repeatedly from the same state.
Training needs an on-policy algorithmic expert; tasks with only offline human demonstrations are not covered.
Evaluated only in simulation on two tasks, with a small human trial (131 episodes, 11 participants).
